title: Teach or teach not
author: John Wills Lloyd
summary: John Wills Lloyd borrows Yoda's line, there is no try, to argue that teaching should be defined by what learners actually learn. Treating actions as behaviourists do, he says trying is not a behaviour but a myth carried by the language of mentalism, so a teacher either taught something or did not. He ties this to his earlier definition of teaching, which requires an outcome in the learner, either a concept or an operation. Presenting a lesson is the attempt; the evidence that teaching happened lies in the learners' later performance. Lloyd concludes that teachers must accept responsibility when students do not learn and deserve credit and rewards when they do, which he links to professionalising the workforce with evidence-based tools and administrative support. He connects the idea to the maxim, associated with Siegfried Engelmann, that if the child has not learned, the child has not yet been successfully taught, and adds that outcomes must be specified before instruction.
points: Lloyd defines teaching by learner outcomes, so a lesson that was presented but not learned counts as an attempt rather than as teaching.
Treating teaching as communication puts the burden on the teacher: if the student does not get it, the response is to communicate better and try again.
Accountability cuts both ways, so teachers who take responsibility for failures should also receive credit and rewards for successes.
Professionalising the workforce requires evidence-based tools and administrator support, not only willingness to accept responsibility.
Claiming credit for a student's growth requires outcomes and measures specified in advance, with performance recorded before and after instruction.
quotes: Trying is a myth foisted on us by the language of mentalism. As children, we are taught to “try.
If one thinks of actions in the way that behaviorists think of them, one realizes that there is no “try.” Trying is not an action, not a behavior.
A key idea in that earlier post was that there had to be outcomes. That is, the learner had to learn something.
Teaching is, fundamentally, communicating. The teacher’s job is to communicate something (concept or operation) to the student.
If the student does not “get it,” has the teacher communicated? Heck no. The teacher did not communicate it. Try again! And do a better job of communicating.
If teachers have to take the heat when students do not learn, they also get to take credit when students do learn.
Acknowledging responsibility for one’s failures and resolving to improve outcomes are hallmarks of professionalism.
Remember, please, that outcomes should be specified in advance of learning.
